analysis.one_liner: Taxes big financial trades to fund infrastructure, health, college, and climate programs.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it never received a hearing, vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would place a small tax on Wall Street trading: half a cent on every dollar of stock sales, a tenth of a cent on bonds, and a fraction of a cent on derivatives. High-income households would pay it; households earning under $50,000 ($75,000 for couples) would get the tax fully refunded. The bill's findings say the money would go to free college, child care, expanded Medicare and Medicaid, infrastructure, clean energy, and global health programs. It never moved past the introductory stage.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, lower- and middle-income households would benefit twice: they would be exempt from the tax through a full credit, and the revenue would fund programs the bill names, including free college, expanded Medicare and Medicaid, child care, housing assistance, and climate investments. The bill's stated rationale is that rapid-fire speculative trading, not long-term investing, bears most of the cost [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The tax is charged on each transfer of stocks (0.5%), bonds (0.10%), and derivatives (0.005%), so it falls heaviest on frequent traders rather than on someone who buys and holds [S3].
Households with income under $50,000 ($75,000 joint) get a credit for the full amount of the tax they paid, so the smallest investors pay nothing [S2] [S3].
The bill directs the revenue toward free college, student debt relief, expanded Medicare and Medicaid, child care, housing assistance, infrastructure, clean energy, and global health programs [S3].
The bill's findings argue the tax would curb high-frequency trading, which it says can make up as much as 70% of the market and contributes to price volatility [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The cost falls on frequent traders, brokerages, clearing houses, and high-income investors, who pay the tax on each covered trade; large financial firms that trade in high volume would bear the most. Retail investors in higher-income brackets who trade regularly would also pay, and economists generally expect part of the tax to be passed through in trading costs and slightly lower prices [S3].

drawbacks.text: The tax applies to any trade where either party is a U.S. person, even trades executed abroad, which critics argued could push trading overseas and cost financial-sector jobs [S3].

A trading tax raises the cost of dealing for everyone in the market, including pension funds and retirement savers above the income threshold, and part of the cost typically lands on them through wider spreads and higher fees.
The bill includes penalties for failing to report covered transactions and requires brokers and trading facilities to collect the tax, adding compliance work across the financial industry [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a large redistributive proposal: a few tenths of a percent on trades raises substantial revenue that the bill would spend on programs for low- and middle-income families, while households under the income caps pay nothing. The honest objections are that trading could move offshore despite the bill's anti-avoidance provisions, and that some of the tax would be passed through to retirement savers and ordinary investors above the income threshold. As written, the direct household benefit (the full credit) is narrow, and the main benefit to ordinary people runs through how the revenue is spent.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up; it died there when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Sanders introduced the bill on April 3, 2017, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S1] [S5].
That referral was the last action on the bill; no hearing, markup, floor vote, or further committee action is recorded [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2019, so the bill expired without ever reaching the Senate floor [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-volume trading firms and the securities industry were better off because the tax never advanced: their trading costs stayed unchanged. Ordinary households gained nothing either, since the proposed credits and program funding never materialized, but they lost nothing directly either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Trading firms; the tax never advanced

against.name: Senate Finance Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after its referral [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by an Independent and drew a single Democratic cosponsor with no Republican support on record; it never reached a vote, so no party breakdown exists.

industries.note: The tax would directly cut into revenue from high-volume trading by charging a fee on every covered transaction, with the heaviest burden on hedge funds and other frequent traders. From the public's side, the revenue funds programs for ordinary households, so the industry's cost is the public's gain.

They would be required to collect and remit the tax on transactions they handle, a compliance cost, and could lose some trading volume if activity shifts to markets abroad. Retail investors below the income caps would be made whole, so the direct burden on small customers is limited by design.

industries.industry: Public universities, health systems, and infrastructure contractors
industries.note: The bill directs its revenue toward college affordability, expanded Medicare and Medicaid, child care, housing, and infrastructure, which would be new funding streams for these sectors and the households they serve.
